prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to reach the 10^-18 regime of frequency accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my preferred single-part prize, and I have tested the case against the chair's questions rather than against the count of first places. The achievement is a specific, datable idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which cancels the lattice light shift so that very many neutral atoms are interrogated in parallel) joined to its decisive realisation (Ye's strontium clock at about 1e-18, with the many-body and dense-lattice physics that followed). It has been reproduced and surpassed in several laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg and checked through fibre and free-space clock comparisons, and the downstream results are already realised: bounds on drifting constants, dark-matter and new-physics searches, and relativistic geodesy at the millimetre scale. As an experimentalist I apply one test to an instrument-level prize, namely whether it opens a measurement regime that was not accessible before, and a clock that resolves the gravitational redshift across a millimetre does so. On the overlap question, the 2005 prize covered the comb that makes optical frequencies countable and the 2012 prize covered control of single quantum systems; neither covers trapping a large neutral ensemble without a light shift, which is where the statistical gain behind the stability comes from. The citation is worded around that lattice architecture and the 10^-18 regime so that it is not a verdict on optical clocks in general. Among the three leading ballots, this has the cleanest attribution and the most settled interpretation.
statement.case_against: My position is weaker than my first-round statement implied in three respects. First, whether a record-precision clock is a discovery or invention in the statutory sense remains a real judgment call, and Mehlig and Danielsson are right that its main output so far is a better instrument plus tests of constants at smaller uncertainty, not a new class of phenomena. Second, the credit tail is real: Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, Derevianko, the Yb and Hg groups and Ye's JILA collaborators are not named, and the Katori and Ye groups contested who first reached the 1e-18 regime, so the two-name split is defensible but not obviously equal. Third, the SI second has not been redefined, so the full payoff is still prospective, and I would not call the case closed on that basis. A committee that weights conceptual breadth over attribution clarity, as Eriksson, Johansson and Mehlig do, can reasonably reach B045, and I do not think that choice would be unscientific.

responses.point: Kroll supports B022 with Katori and Ye, accepts the overlap with 2005 and 2012 as answerable by narrow wording, and discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory with Ye as a Hall-lineage scientist.
responses.response: We agree on the configuration and the narrow wording, but on the chair's question I think the Hall connection should be handled as a disclosed bias and not as formal recusal: a past stay in a laboratory two steps removed from Ye, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, is a lineage tie. The practical safeguard is that B022 does not depend on Kroll's vote, since Lindroth, Olsson and I reached it independently and our reasons differ in emphasis. I would ask Kroll to say whether he would hold his ranking if the committee asked him to abstain on the final B022 vote, because that tells us how much of the support is judgment and how much is familiarity.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B045 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) because topological band theory changed how a field classifies matter, and he describes the lattice clock mainly as a better instrument.
responses.response: I accept the category objection more than I did in round one: the clock is an advance in what can be measured, not a new class of phenomena, and that is the weakest part of my case. But you also say the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is why the HgTe experiment was done and cannot be repaired because Zhang has died. If a prize must be reworded to avoid the missing name, then its attribution is no longer cleaner than the clock's, whose omitted names are later and parallel contributors rather than the originator of the tested prediction. I would take the breadth argument seriously if the citation could be limited to quantum spin Hall and Z2 without that gap, and I am not yet persuaded that it can.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B045 first, arguing that a lattice clock is a precision gain within a field recognised in 2005 and 2012 whereas band topology introduced a classification principle, and that the 2016 prize concerned different physics.
responses.response: Your reading of 2016 is persuasive and I withdraw the suggestion that the overlap is by itself a reason to wait: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz concerned phase transitions and Hall plateaux, while time-reversal-invariant helical edge states are a separate mechanism. That moves B045 from a prize I regarded as partly pre-honoured to a fully credible alternative, and it is why it remains my first alternative. Where I still differ is the claim that precision within an honoured field is automatically lesser. The same argument was available against many accepted prizes, and the question should be whether the lattice idea is new, which I think it is. I also note that your own uncertainty about whether 3D topological insulators belong is the point on which the B045 citation could still fragment.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B045 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, would address the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap in the wording of the citation, and names B022 as a clean fallback he would not block.
responses.response: I appreciate that you name B022 as an acceptable fallback, and I agree that Mele belongs with Kane if topology is chosen. I would press on one point: the citation can say that the prize is for the prediction and first observation of the quantum spin Hall effect, but it cannot make the omitted HgTe proposers appear in the credited list, and the committee should be prepared to hear that criticism publicly. The distinction between the shared topological theme and the distinct Z2 mechanism is well taken, and it means I no longer treat 2016 as an obstacle. What remains between us is how much weight to give a known, permanent credit gap against breadth of influence.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B030 as a rare prediction followed by an unexpected experiment, and holds that the flat-band origin is stable even though the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: The separation you draw between the discovery and the mechanism is fair, and I accept that earlier prizes in superconductivity and quantum Hall physics were not delayed until the mechanism was fully understood. My remaining concern is the credit and the age of the field: Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young and the Lopes dos Santos and Santos theory lines sit outside the three names, and the sensitivity to twist-angle disorder means the reproducibility record is shorter than the clock record. I keep B030 as my second alternative, and I would expect it to become a stronger first choice within a few years if the correlated phases are settled.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B022 first but records that the allocation is less clean than the supplied credit string suggests and that she may be inflated by disciplinary closeness.
responses.response: Your candour about disciplinary bias is the right one and I share it in kind, since an instrument builder is predisposed to value an instrument result. In answer to the chair's question on how to divide credit, I would treat Katori's magic-wavelength proposal as the originating idea and Ye's group as the decisive demonstration of the regime, giving them near-equal weight, and I would ask you whether you accept that division. Your concern about NIST, PTB, SYRTE and RIKEN is why the citation has to name the lattice architecture and the 10^-18 regime, not clocks in general.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the magic-wavelength lattice clock as a discovery or invention distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 lineage, which the narrow citation is intended to settle but cannot settle for every member.
How to divide credit between Katori's concept and Ye's realisation, and whether the Lemonde, Takamoto, Yb and Hg groups make a two-name prize unfair.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second strengthens the case or argues for waiting, which I consider not a precondition.

Whether a B045 citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification can stand without the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, which would change my relative ranking of B022 and B045.
statement.conflict_note: I report no conflict on B022, B045 or B030: my documented background is astroparticle instrumentation (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO), with no documented tie to Katori, Ye or the credited names on the other leading ballots. A connection would arise only if B046 or B002 were taken up, and I would flag it then. On Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory link, I consider it a disclosed bias to be weighed, not a formal conflict, and the committee should decide it openly.
